Hermes Agent OS (imshubhamsocial/dotfiles-hermes at commit dfc45ab, validated against raw execution trajectories in imshubhamsocial/hermes-tests at commit 113b0b4) is formally granted Production Green-Light Certification across all 54 chronological implementation phases1. Cross-auditing the live configuration, hardware telemetry, and raw benchmark logs indicates that all historical architectural mandates from GDR1 through GDR29 operate harmoniously without regression inside the physical envelope of the discrete NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050 Laptop GPU (6,144 MiB physical GDDR6, strict ≤5,800.0 MiB safety ceiling leaving ≥344 MiB for CUDA runtime contexts, Disp.A: Off) and AMD Ryzen 5 7430U CPU1. By decommissioning passive, schema-only Layer A completion benchmarks on Port 8138 (which yield false-negative 0.000 scores on autonomous gateways that execute tools internally) and transitioning release gating to the **Layer B Agent Harness Gauntlet**, Phase 54 validates end-to-end autonomous tool execution, multi-turn policy adherence, and 128K context stability (-c 131072 with Google TurboQuant q4\_0 KV cache)2.  
Across the three evaluated substrates, unsloth/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-UD-Q4\_K\_XL.gguf (Candidate 3\) is certified as the Tier 1B Primary Agent OS Champion, and xbill9/gemma-4-E4B-it-qat-q4\_0-exact.gguf (Candidate 2\) is certified as the Tier 1A Coding & AST Specialist, while Google's official gemma-4-E4B-it-qat-q4\_0-gguf (Candidate 1\) is permanently decommissioned3. Independent mathematical and trajectory forensics indicate that Candidate 1's 0.0% collapse on Tau-Bench Retail was not caused by port clashes or environment misconfiguration, but by a quantization grid-scaling shift in Google's official GGUF export that elevates mean Kullback-Leibler Divergence (KLD) from bf16 by 34.19x (0.035254 vs. 0.001031 in Candidate 2\) and reduces top-1 token match fidelity to 90.64%, yielding a 74.74% cumulative probability of mutating a 14-token tool-and-order identifier sequence3. Furthermore, to restore high-throughput speculative decoding on Candidate 3 without triggering the 1,070.08 MiB CUDA graph out-of-memory (OOM) crash observed with the 381 MiB Q8\_0 DFlash drafter, this report specifies the local conversion workflow for a 205.38 MiB Q4\_0 or 220.42 MiB Q4\_K\_M DFlash drafter paired with GGML\_CUDA\_DISABLE\_GRAPHS=1 and \--spec-draft-n-ubatch 64, projecting 60.6 to 77.3 tokens/sec within a 5,417.4 MiB to 5,481.4 MiB active VRAM footprint (+318.6 MiB to \+382.6 MiB safety margin below 5,800.0 MiB)4.  
Finally, this consultation resolves the apparent paradox between Jake Van Clief and David McDermott's 2,000–8,000 token working context rule (arXiv:2603.16021v2) and the 128K physical KV cache buffer, while establishing a universal tripartite folder standard (invariants.md, rules.md, references.md) and a v45 declarative config.yaml upgrade10. In Interpretable Context Methodology (ICM / Model Workspace Protocol), the 2,000–8,000 token bound is not a virtual sliding-window truncation of conversation history; it is **structural context scoping by construction** across a five-layer filesystem hierarchy designed to prevent transformer attention dilution ("lost in the middle"), while the 128K physical context buffer serves as an ephemeral execution arena for high-volume tool payloads, compiler dumps, and multi-turn ReAct traces10. While Van Clief and McDermott note that their foundational paper's practitioner telemetry (52 community members, 33 active multi-stage workspace users) relied on qualitative interviews rather than controlled A/B logging across all tasks, the Phase 54 empirical gauntlet in hermes-tests provides concrete, reproducible benchmark verification of ICM's architectural invariants on local 4B hardware3.

### **1.2 Harmonization Verification Across Subsystem Boundaries**

A critical concern in multi-epoch systems engineering is whether late-stage optimizations (Epochs 4 and 5\) silently degrade early-stage foundations (Epochs 1–3). Empirical telemetry from the Phase 54 evaluation confirms three cross-epoch synergies operating across the hardware and software stack1.  
First, **Memory Graph and CPU Embedding Isolation (Epochs 1, 2, and 5\)** prevents GPU memory contention. By binding local-embedding-cpu (embeddinggemma-2-q8\_0 with matryoshka\_dim: 256\) to Port 8139 on CPU cores 6–11 while pinning llama-server inference to CPU cores 0–5 via taskset \-c 0-5, the OpenViking memory graph (Port 1933\) performs vector indexing and memory extraction with zero CUDA context overhead on the discrete RTX 30501. Alongside desktop compositor isolation on the integrated AMD Radeon GPU (consuming 6 MiB with Disp.A: Off on the NVIDIA dGPU) and 15.3 GiB of compressed zram swap plus a 2 GiB btrfs NOCOW swapfile (/var/swap/swapfile), this partitioning allowed the 128K TurboQuant KV cache on Port 8138 to claim 4,169 MiB on Candidate 2 and 4,975 MiB on Candidate 3 while maintaining a steady 56°C thermal profile under load1.  
Second, **Three-Tier Prompt Assembly and Prefix Cache Stability (Epochs 3 and 4\)** work together to accelerate multi-turn inference. Upstream NousResearch/hermes-agent (agent/system\_prompt.py) partitions system prompts into stable (SOUL.md identity and core tool guidance), context (AGENTS.md and workspace rules), and volatile (per-turn dynamic state) layers specifically to maximize KV prefix caching21. Because Epoch 4 consolidated orchestration into immutable Layer 0 (AGENTS.md) and Layer 1 (CONTEXT.md) markdown files, llama-server achieved a 99.8% prefix cache hit rate on Candidate 3 and 99.2% on Candidate 2 across multi-turn benchmark trajectories1.  
Third, **Zero-Bespoke Gateway Purity and Layer B ReAct Routing (Epochs 4 and 5\)** preserve upstream maintainability during external benchmarking. Rather than modifying upstream gateway/platforms/api\_server.py to bypass client tool stripping (Upstream Issue \#28825)—which would have violated the GDR28 Zero-Bespoke Imperative by dirtying the .hermes/hermes-agent submodule—Phase 54 deployed tau\_bench.run \--agent-strategy react (ChatReActAgent) alongside a dual-port litellm routing harness2. This preserved 100% upstream code purity while accurately evaluating multi-turn database mutations2.

## **2\. Deep Literature and Commercial Analysis of Jake Van Clief's ICM**

### **2.1 Definitive Resolution of the 2,000–8,000 Token Working Context vs. 128K Physical Buffer Paradox**

A central theoretical and operational question in GDR30 is why Jake Van Clief and David McDermott's *Interpretable Context Methodology: Folder Structure as Agentic Architecture* (arXiv:2603.16021v2, March 18, 2026; earlier referred to as the *Model Workspace Protocol* or MWP) and its accompanying icm-architect specification mandate keeping an agent's active working context between **2,000 and 8,000 tokens per stage** when modern local and frontier models support 128K to 1M+ token context windows10.  
Cross-referencing Van Clief and McDermott's primary paper (arXiv:2603.16021v2)12, the RinDig/Interpretable-Context-Methodology reference repository26, and the RinDig/icm-architect specification (SKILL.md Invariant 7 and Walk Test)27 resolves this paradox: ICM does NOT use a virtual sliding window over conversation history (rejecting Hypothesis A); instead, it enforces Stage-Scoped Progressive Context Disclosure over an Externalized Filesystem State Machine (confirming and extending Hypothesis B)10.  
First, ICM practices **prevention rather than compression** to defeat "lost in the middle" attention decay12. Van Clief and McDermott explicitly cite Liu et al.'s finding that transformer models suffer severe recall and instruction-following degradation when relevant rules are buried in the middle of long, noisy context windows12. While post-hoc prompt compression algorithms (such as Jiang et al., which achieve up to 20x token reduction after loading) attempt to shrink bloated contexts, ICM avoids loading irrelevant tokens in the first place12. In the paper's sample content production workflow (evaluated qualitatively on Claude Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6), a monolithic single-context comparison passed \~42,000 tokens—most of which were unfollowed instructions from non-executing stages and already-consumed intermediate artifacts—whereas the ICM stage-scoped workflow loaded roughly **4,900 to 5,600 tokens** at each focused stage14. This empirical measurement sits squarely inside the **2,000 to 8,000 token** healthy operating range codified in icm-architect Invariant 7 and community technical analyses13.  
Second, ICM enforces **structural separation of attention modes between Layer 3 constraints and Layer 4 inputs**12. Van Clief and McDermott note that language models must apply two distinct types of attention to context: *Reference Material (Layer 3\)* must be internalized as behavioral constraints ("here are the rules, follow them"), whereas *Working Artifacts (Layer 4\)* must be processed as mutable inputs ("here is the input, transform it")12. When both are dumped into an unstructured 50K+ prompt, the model frequently confuses descriptive input data with prescriptive instructions12. By loading only \~1,300 to 1,600 tokens across Layers 0–2 (roughly 800 tokens for Layer 0 identity, 300 tokens for Layer 1 routing, and 200–500 tokens for the Layer 2 stage contract), 500 to 2,000 tokens of selective Layer 3 references, and the immediate Layer 4 input artifact, the signal-to-noise ratio remains high12. Citing research by Jones and Kelly at Anthropic, the authors also apply this stage-scoping principle to tool definitions so that an agent only sees the tools required for the active stage12. Furthermore, if an orchestrating agent delegates sub-tasks to smaller specialist models, the folder hierarchy itself supplies the scoped context for those sub-agent delegations without requiring framework-level message-passing code12.  
Third, in an autonomous operating system like Hermes, **the 128K physical buffer (-c 131072\) remains essential as an intra-stage execution arena**3. The 2,000–8,000 token ICM discipline governs the **initial Stage Entry Frame** (Layers 0–4 loaded from disk at the start of a stage)4. Once the stage begins executing a multi-turn tool loop—such as Stage 03 (03-execute) running ast-grep, reading C or Python source files, inspecting compiler diagnostics, or executing a 17-to-25-turn ReAct database interaction in Tau-Bench—the transient intra-stage execution trace (ephemeral tool outputs, file diffs, and reasoning blocks) expands dynamically within the physical KV cache3. As observed in GDR29, if the physical engine or agent\_init.py is capped at 32K, burst tool outputs or multi-turn ReAct traces trigger hard context-overflow crashes1. Once the stage concludes and writes its clean deliverable to output/, the transient multi-turn execution trace is discarded, and the next stage initializes with a clean 2,000–8,000 token working context12.

### **2.2 Jake Van Clief's Commercial Ecosystem, Tooling, and Monetization Architecture**

An examination of academic publications, corporate documentation, community platforms, and GitHub repositories shows how Jake Van Clief (an 8-year U.S. Marine Corps avionics and cryptographic technician on F-35/F-18 platforms, University of Edinburgh MSc in Future Governance researcher, and Founder & CEO of **Eduba**) and his Chief Architect **David McDermott** (MS Computer Science, former BAE Systems, Epic Games, and Derivco engineer) commercialize ICM13.  
Van Clief positions ICM and Eduba (eduba.io) against code-heavy multi-agent frameworks (such as LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen) by targeting two widespread problems in enterprise AI adoption: low post-training retention and the coordination overhead of multi-agent swarms26. While multi-agent frameworks are suitable for high-concurrency or real-time dynamic branching systems, Van Clief and McDermott argue that sequential, human-reviewed enterprise workflows do not need complex framework code that turns operators into "messenger boys" copying context between isolated bots12. By treating the filesystem as a state machine and plain Markdown as the universal interface (drawing on 1970s Bell Labs Unix pipelines, David Parnas's modular decomposition, Stuart Feldman's Make build graphs, and Donald Knuth's literate programming), ICM delivers *glass-box interpretability* and *allodial ownership*—clients hold plain folders in their own Git repositories with zero vendor lock-in12. On its corporate website, Eduba cites client testimonials reporting a **95% 30-day team retention rate** (compared to a \~10% industry average) across enterprise training and consulting engagements with organizations such as Pacific Life, IAG, Colgate-Palmolive, KPMG UK, and Flagler College, alongside research adoption at the University of Edinburgh's Neuropolitics Lab, ICR Research, and the Academy of International Affairs in Bonn13.  
Rather than charging licensing fees for the folder methodology itself—a practice ecosystem partners like Ryan "RyMac" McKinney (filesnfolders.com) explicitly critique as charging "\$5,000 for a text file and a folder structure"33—Van Clief releases the core ICM paper (arXiv:2603.16021v2), reference workspaces (RinDig/Interpretable-Context-Methodology), and agent restructuring skill (RinDig/icm-architect, with 2.1k+ GitHub stars) free under the **MIT License**12. Commercial monetization operates across a three-tier ecosystem13:

| Commercial Tier | Platform / Entity | Core Offering & Target Audience | Monetization & Pricing Structure |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Tier 1: Open-Source Protocol & Community Funnel** | Clief Notes (Substack & Skool CL001) \+ Partner Hubs (filesnfolders.com)32 | Open-source MIT repositories (RinDig), free starter kits, and a public Skool community (reported between 12,500+ on eduba.io and 52,897 members on third-party directory skoolmakers.com)28. | Free entry tier for protocol, paper, and starter folders; paid monthly membership tier in Clief Notes for live coaching, workspace audits, and practitioner Q\&A30. |

In commercial engagements, Eduba executes a 5-stage delivery sequence called **Computational Orchestration** (*1\. Learn the Workflow → 2\. Sort the Work → 3\. Train People to Build → 4\. Build What Makes Sense → 5\. Govern What Works*) that operationalizes Van Clief's **60/30/10 Principle**32. In this framework, 60% of a production system consists of deterministic infrastructure (traditional software, databases, compilers, and shell scripts that handle mechanical work without AI), 30% consists of structured markdown orchestration (folder hierarchy, routing tables, and stage contracts that supply directional motive and context scoping), and only 10% consists of AI cognition12. By sorting tasks into traditional software, rule-based logic, AI, or "do not build" before writing a single prompt, Eduba prevents the common commercial failure mode of forcing the 10% AI layer to perform deterministic tasks that belong in the 60% infrastructure layer32.

## **3\. Standardized Universal Repository and Benchmark Scaffolding**

### **3.1 Synthesizing Tripartite Contracts (invariants.md, rules.md, references.md) with ICM Layers 0–4**

In his architectural writings and workspace audits, Jake Van Clief emphasizes that autonomous agents fail when constraints, procedures, and domain schemas are mixed together in a single sprawling prompt file, or when the same rule is duplicated across multiple files—violating the *"One Fact, One Home"* (canonical source) rule10. When an agent reads a long file containing both non-negotiable security boundaries and optional formatting suggestions, transformer attention can treat hard boundaries as soft guidelines10.  
To maintain architectural consistency across all Hermes workspaces, general tasks, and Layer B benchmark gauntlets, every operational scope isolates its Layer 2 and Layer 3 context into three specialized files alongside CONTEXT.md10. First, **invariants.md (The "Never" Layer — Hard Operational & Mathematical Bounds)** acts as a Layer 2/3 hard constraint contract (≤80 lines) defining falsifiable, machine-verifiable invariants that must hold true before, during, and after stage execution10. Examples include discrete GPU VRAM ≤5,800.0 MiB via NVML, .hermes/hermes-agent submodule git status \--porcelain returning empty, active stage prompt token count ≤8,000 tokens, and Port 8642 (Agent) and Port 20128 (Customer) never sharing an endpoint10. Violating any constraint in invariants.md triggers an immediate abort in contract.sh10.  
Second, **rules.md (The "Always & Ask First" Layer — Procedural Directives & Heuristics)** serves as the Layer 2/3 procedural protocol (≤120 lines) specifying execution heuristics, tool invocation order, linting/compilation flags (ruff check, pyright, gcc \-Wall), anti-rationalization tables, anti-sycophancy directives, and the Two-Strike Tabu Rule (if a tool call or AST query fails twice with identical parameters, halt and reformulate rather than looping)3.  
Third, **references.md (The "Knowledge" Layer — Machine-Readable Schemas & Pointers)** serves as the Layer 3 static factory reference (capped at ≤200 lines per file per ICM specification; split into modular files inside references/ if larger and loaded via Selective Section Routing)10. It stores factual domain data, port registries, mock database schemas, API payload formats, and product catalogs10. By keeping references.md strictly descriptive with zero imperative instructions, the language model never confuses reference data with execution commands10.

### **3.4 Canonical Stage Contract Template with the 4th Verify Section**

To operationalize Van Clief and McDermott's solution to the U-shaped intervention curve (arXiv:2603.16021v2 Section 4.4 and Section 6.2), every CONTEXT.md inside stages/ and benchmarks/ adopts the following 4-part structure (strictly ≤80 lines)12:

# **Stage 03: Execute (Surgical Code Mutation & AST Verification)**

## **Inputs**

| Source | File / Location | Section / Scope | Why |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Stage 02 Plan | ../02-plan/output/plan.md | Full file | Approved file mutation targets |
| Stage 01 Spec | ../01-spec/output/spec.md | \#\# Acceptance Criteria | Cross-stage alignment anchor |
| Stage Invariants | ./invariants.md | Full file | Hard VRAM & Zero-Bespoke bounds |
| Stage Rules | ./rules.md | \#\# AST & Compiler Protocol | Mandatory pre-commit checks |
| Port & AST Ref | ./references.md | \#\# AST Pattern Signatures | Syntax templates for ast-grep |

## **Process**

> 1. Read ../02-plan/output/plan.md and verify all target paths exist.  
> 2. Query target syntax trees using ast-grep prior to any file mutation.  
> 3. Apply minimal surgical diffs; embed provenance tags (\# icm-trace: SPEC-XX).  
> 4. Run language-specific diagnostics (pyright, ruff check, or gcc \-Wall \-O2).  
> 5. Execute the \#\# Verify alignment audit below before saving to ./output/.

## **Verify**

* **Cross-Stage Trace**: Compare every modified function against ../01-spec/output/spec.md\#Acceptance-Criteria (Stage 01\) to prevent non-adjacent stage drift.  
* **Invariant Gate**: Confirm git status \--porcelain .hermes/hermes-agent is empty and scripts/ contains zero files.  
* **Two-Strike Tabu**: If any compiler or AST check fails twice consecutively, halt and write a diagnostic blocker to ./output/execution\_audit.md.

## **Outputs**

| Artifact | Location | Format |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Execution Audit & Diff Log | ./output/execution\_audit.md | Markdown with \#SPEC-XX source-map provenance |

### **4.1 Independent Task-by-Task Comparative Autopsy**

An audit of the raw execution trajectories in imshubhamsocial/hermes-tests/logs/gdr30\_harness\_evals and BENCHMARK\_ANALYSIS\_REPORT.md details the exact behavioral divergence across the three 128K substrates1.  
In **Track 1: In-Repo Autonomous Coding & CLI Evaluation (make run-eval / fibonacci.c)**, the harness invokes hermes \--in tests/ast\_grep\_eval \-z "Search calculate\_fibonacci using ast-grep and compile with gcc"2. **Candidate 1 (google/gemma-4-E4B-it-qat-q4\_0-gguf)** executed ast-grep \--pattern 'calculate\_fibonacci(\$\$\$)' tests/ast\_grep\_eval/fibonacci.c, inspected long long calculate\_fibonacci(int n), compiled /tmp/fibonacci with gcc \-O2, and verified Fibonacci(10) \= 55 (Exit Code 0\)3. Because make run-eval is a short, 4-step single-goal interaction (\~2K context), Candidate 1's logit perturbations did not cascade into tool failure3. **Candidate 2 (xbill9/gemma-4-E4B-it-qat-q4\_0-exact.gguf)** displayed notable metacognitive grounding: it noticed that earlier prompt history referenced Python AST flags while the target artifact was fibonacci.c, emitting the thought trace *"The target file is in C, whereas python AST grep flags were referenced in earlier history. GCC cannot compile Python source without Cython. In **Track 2: Sierra Research Tau-Bench Retail ReAct Gauntlet (Tasks 0–4)**, customer simulation queries were routed to OmniRoute Port 20128 (frontier-fleet) and support agent queries to Hermes Gateway Port 8642 (hermes-agent)3. ### **4.2 Mathematical Analysis of Candidate 1's Failure: QAT Grid Shift and KLD Compounding**

To determine whether Candidate 1 (google/gemma-4-E4B-it-qat-q4\_0-gguf, 5.15 GB remote file / 4.9 GiB) failed due to intrinsic quantization errors rather than environment artifacts, we examine the tensor-level construction documented in xbill9/gemma-4-E4B-it-qat-q4\_0-exact-gguf7.  
During Google DeepMind's Quantization-Aware Training (google/gemma-4-E4B-it-qat-q4\_0-unquantized), weights in every 32-element block were constrained to a symmetric 4-bit integer grid (-8 to \+7) multiplied by a trained step scale7. However, when Google exported the official GGUF (gemma-4-E4B\_q4\_0-it.gguf), standard llama.cpp Q4\_0 quantization computed each block's scale by dividing the block's largest magnitude by 87. Because QAT frequently places a block's largest magnitude on a lower quantization level (such as 5, 6, or 7), dividing by 8 shifted the entire 32-element block off the trained QAT grid7. By contrast, xbill9 recovered each block's actual trained step (checking integer divisors 8 down to 1 and refining via least squares), matching 96.81% of bf16 source values bit-for-bit after bf16 rounding7. Additionally, Google's official GGUF stored the 3.49 billion embedding values (token\_embd and per\_layer\_token\_embd) in Q6\_K and per\_layer\_model\_proj in F16 (5,154,941,280 bytes; 5,271 MiB active VRAM at 68°C), whereas xbill9 stored all 342 layer matrices, per\_layer\_model\_proj, and both embedding tables on the trained Q4\_0 grid (4,215,695,712 bytes) and allowed the 1.59 GB per\_layer\_token\_embd tensor to be lazily read via mmap from system RAM, cutting active 128K VRAM by 1,102 MiB down to 4,169 MiB and boosting prompt processing past 2,000 t/s3.  
In xbill9's CPU verification benchmarks against the unquantized bf16 QAT checkpoint, Google's official Q4\_0 GGUF exhibited a **mean KL divergence of 0.035254 ± 0.000773** (99th percentile KLD: 0.215774) and a top-1 token match rate of ![][image3] (90.64 ± 0.46%), whereas xbill9's exact Q4\_0 GGUF achieved a **mean KL divergence of 0.001031 ± 0.000053** (99th percentile KLD: 0.008396 — **34.19x lower mean KLD** and **25.70x lower 99th-percentile KLD**) and a top-1 token match rate of ![][image4] (98.41 ± 0.20%)4.  
In natural language prose, a 9.36% per-token flip rate (![][image5]) merely substitutes a near-synonym. In a deterministic ReAct JSON action call, however, every character in a tool name (find\_user\_id\_by\_name\_zip, ![][image6] subword/underscore tokens) and an order ID (\#W2378156, ![][image6] digit/symbol tokens) must be emitted with zero token flips (![][image7] exact identifier tokens)3. Modeling the cumulative probability of emitting an ![][image8]\-token identifier sequence without a single top-1 logit flip as ![][image9] yields the exact failure probabilities across all three identifier lengths4:

| Identifier Sequence & Token Length (NNN) | Candidate 1 (google Official QAT, p1=0.9064p\_1 \= 0.9064p1​=0.9064) Exact Survival (p1Np\_1^Np1N​) | Candidate 1 Identifier Mutation Risk (1−p1N1 \- p\_1^N1−p1N​) | Candidate 2 (xbill9 Exact QAT, p2=0.9841p\_2 \= 0.9841p2​=0.9841) Exact Survival (p2Np\_2^Np2N​) | Candidate 2 Identifier Mutation Risk (1−p2N1 \- p\_2^N1−p2N​) | Observed Trajectory Behavior in hermes-tests |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |

### **4.3 NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt Speculative Decoding & Q4 DFlash Drafter Feasibility Study**

To restore high-speed speculative decoding on **Candidate 3 (unsloth/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-UD-Q4\_K\_XL.gguf)** without breaching the 5,800.0 MiB VRAM ceiling, we examine the architecture of NVIDIA's companion drafter (nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-4GB-DFlash and Unsloth's dflash-NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-Q8\_0.gguf) and the mechanics of the 1,070.08 MiB cudaMalloc crash6.

#### **1\. Architectural Anatomy of the DFlash Drafter (360.48M Parameters)**

Inspection of the nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-4GB-DFlash model card and technical report (NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-4GB-Technical-Report.pdf) establishes the exact tensor structure of the DFlash speculator8. The draft model consists of 5 Qwen3-style transformer decoder layers containing 360,480,000 parameters (360.48M)8. Crucially, the DFlash GGUF **contains no token\_embd or output head tensors**; at runtime inside llama-server (b11808+), it dynamically shares the 262,144-token embedding table and output head of the target Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B model8. During inference, the drafter captures hidden states from 5 layers of the target model and applies **sliding-window attention over the most recent 1,024 tokens**, proposing up to **7 draft tokens** (in an 8-token verification block) in a single non-causal forward pass8.  
Regarding published checkpoints, official nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-4GB-DFlash (Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-DFlash-BF16.gguf) and lmstudio-community/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-DFlash-GGUF provide the unquantized BF16 file at **736,812,096 bytes (736.81 MB / 702.68 MiB)**8, while unsloth/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-GGUF provides dflash-NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-Q8\_0.gguf at **399 MB decimal (380.5 MiB / \~381 MiB binary)**6. No pre-built Q4\_0 or Q4\_K\_M GGUF of the Bolt E4B DFlash drafter is currently hosted in nvidia/, unsloth/, ggml-org/, or lmstudio-community/ (which only host BF16, Q8\_0, and NVFP4)42. However, because the DFlash drafter is already formatted as a standard 5-layer GGUF in BF16 and Q8\_0, **it can be quantized locally using llama-quantize** in the same manner as dflash-Muse-Glimmer-30B-Q4\_K\_M.gguf and Alittlehammmer/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-DFlash-GGUF:Q4\_K\_M53.

#### **2\. Root Cause of the 1,070.08 MiB OOM & Two Critical llama.cpp Bugs**

When Candidate 3 (4,956 MiB idle footprint at 128K context) was launched with dflash-NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-Q8\_0.gguf (381 MiB), llama-server crashed attempting to allocate a **1,070.08 MiB CUDA graph/compute buffer**3. Three compounding factors caused this allocation spike:  
First, **Dual-Graph Capture Overhead and the llama.cpp Issue \#25835 CUDA Graph Leak** inflated VRAM demand. When speculative decoding (--spec-type draft-dflash or draft-mtp) is active with CUDA Graphs enabled (the default in llama-server), ggml-cuda reserves large staging and graph-capture buffers for both the target verification batch (-ub 512\) and the non-causal block-diffusion draft graph (1,070.08 MiB)6. Even more critically, as documented in ggml-org/llama.cpp **Issue \#25835** (verified across RTX 4090 and V100 on Linux and Windows), **combining CUDA Graphs with DFlash or MTP speculative decoding triggers a linear driver-level VRAM leak of \+7.97 MiB per request**, which crashes long-running servers with cudaMalloc failed: out of memory9. Setting the environment variable **GGML\_CUDA\_DISABLE\_GRAPHS=1** eliminates both the initial graph reservation spike and the \+7.97 MiB/req leak (reducing drift to \+0.033 MiB/req) with only a \-0.4% to \-2.2% impact on generation tok/s9.  
Second, **Unbounded Draft Physical Micro-Batch (--spec-draft-n-ubatch)** wasted scratch buffer space. By default, \--spec-draft-n-ubatch inherits \--n-ubatch (512), sizing the drafter's compute buffer for 512 parallel tokens even though DFlash drafts a block of 7 tokens (--spec-draft-n-max 7\) after prefill8. Setting \--spec-draft-n-ubatch 64 (or 128\) reduces the draft compute buffer to \~96–145 MiB4.  
Third, **Draft KV Cache Quantization and Attention Rotation (llama.cpp Issue \#25725 / PR \#25823)** must be configured explicitly. Unless \--cache-type-k-draft and \--cache-type-v-draft are passed, llama-server allocates the 5-layer DFlash KV cache in f16 (\~320 MiB)4. Passing \--cache-type-k-draft q8\_0 \--cache-type-v-draft q8\_0 halves the draft KV cache to \~160 MiB4. Ensure llama-server is at build **b11808+**, which includes both DFlash support for Bolt E4B and PR \#25823 (merged in b10068) to rotate injected target KV states when draft KV quantization is active, preventing the 0% acceptance collapse seen in pre-b10068 builds8.

#### **3\. Mathematical VRAM Sizing Matrix (6 Configurations on RTX 3050 6,144 MiB)**

Quantizing the 360,480,000 parameters of the 5-layer DFlash drafter from BF16 (702.68 MiB) or Q8\_0 (381.00 MiB at 8.5 bits/weight) down to 4-bit formats (4.5 bits/weight \= 0.5625 bytes/weight for Q4\_0/IQ4\_NL, or 4.85 bits/weight \= 0.60625 bytes/weight for Q4\_K\_M, plus 12.0 MiB of F32 norms and metadata) yields GGUF weight footprints of **205.38 MiB (215.35 MB) for Q4\_0 / IQ4\_NL** and **220.42 MiB (231.12 MB) for Q4\_K\_M**4:  
![][image12]

| Configuration Strategy | Target \+ 128K KV | Drafter Weights | Draft KV Cache | Compute / Graph Buffer | Total Active VRAM | Margin vs. 5,800 MiB Ceiling (vs. 6,144 MiB Physical) | Projected Speed (RTX 3050\) |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **1\. Failed Phase 54 Attempt** (Q8\_0 Drafter \+ f16 Draft KV \+ Graphs ON)4 | 4,956.0 MiB | 381.0 MiB | 320.0 MiB | 1,070.1 MiB | **6,727.1 MiB** | **\-927.1 MiB** (-583.1 MiB — **OOM CRASH**) | Crashed on load4 |

#### **4\. Actionable CLI Blueprint: Quantizing and Launching the Q4\_0 / Q4\_K\_M DFlash Drafter**

In current llama.cpp (b11808+), legacy flags \--draft-max and \--draft-min have been removed and replaced by \--spec-draft-n-max and \--spec-draft-n-min58, and CUDA graphs are disabled via GGML\_CUDA\_DISABLE\_GRAPHS=19. Furthermore, llama-server supports comma-separated hybrid speculation (--spec-type draft-dflash,ngram-mod), where draftless ngram-mod (\~16 MB host RAM, 0 MiB VRAM) takes precedence on repetitive code/JSON sequences and falls back to draft-dflash for novel tokens56:

Bash  
\# Step 1: Quantize the DFlash Drafter (from NVIDIA BF16 or Unsloth Q8\_0 GGUF) to Q4\_0 (or Q4\_K\_M)  
\# Using Unsloth's published imatrix\_unsloth.gguf (8.87 MB) preserves high acceptance lengths (\~4.62 on code, \~4.89 on extraction, \~5.87 on math)  
llama-quantize \\  
  \--imatrix \~/.hermes/models/imatrix\_unsloth.gguf \\  
  \~/.hermes/models/dflash-NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-Q8\_0.gguf \\  
  \~/.hermes/models/dflash-NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-Q4\_0.gguf \\  
  Q4\_0

\# Step 2: Launch Port 8138 llama-server with Candidate 3 \+ Q4\_0 DFlash \+ N-Gram Hybrid Speculation  
\# Active VRAM settles at \~5,417.4 MiB (+382.6 MiB safety margin below 5,800.0 MiB; \+726.6 MiB below 6,144 MiB)  
GGML\_CUDA\_DISABLE\_GRAPHS=1 taskset \-c 0-5 llama-server \\  
  \-m \~/.hermes/models/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-UD-Q4\_K\_XL.gguf \\  
  \-md \~/.hermes/models/dflash-NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-Q4\_0.gguf \\  
  \--alias nemotron-3.5-bolt-e4b \\  
  \--host 127.0.0.1 \\  
  \--port 8138 \\  
  \-c 131072 \\  
  \-ngl 99 \\  
  \-ngld 99 \\  
  \-fa on \\  
  \-ctk q4\_0 \\  
  \-ctv q4\_0 \\  
  \--cache-type-k-draft q8\_0 \\  
  \--cache-type-v-draft q8\_0 \\  
  \-b 1024 \\  
  \-ub 512 \\  
  \--spec-draft-n-ubatch 64 \\  
  \--spec-type draft-dflash,ngram-mod \\  
  \--spec-draft-n-max 7 \\  
  \--spec-draft-n-min 2 \\  
  \--spec-ngram-mod-n-match 16 \\  
  \--spec-ngram-mod-n-min 16 \\  
  \--spec-ngram-mod-n-max 48 \\  
  \--reasoning auto \\  
  \--jinja

## **5\. Codebase Purity Audit and Upstream Configuration Specifications**

### **5.1 Forensic Codebase Purity Audit (dotfiles-hermes@dfc45ab)**

An audit of the imshubhamsocial/dotfiles-hermes repository artifacts at commit dfc45ab confirms **compliance with the GDR28 Zero-Bespoke Imperative**1.  
First, the **scripts/ directory is verified empty**11. All 17 legacy custom scripts (run\_remediated\_gauntlet.sh, mcp\_ephemeral\_bridge.py, ast\_canonizer.py, epistemic\_scorer.py, etc.) were permanently removed in Phase 53, and no custom \_\_init\_\_.py files or monkey-patches exist in the repository2.  
Second, the **plugins/ directory contains only unmodified, upstream packages**11. The first plugin, **volcengine/OpenViking (openviking v0.5.0 on Port 1933\)**, is the official MIT-licensed hierarchical memory plugin providing viking\_search, viking\_read, viking\_browse, viking\_remember, viking\_forget, and viking\_add\_resource11. Version 0.5.0 resolves overlapping local embedding calls and commits automatically at 20,000 pending tokens or session end20. The second plugin, **anpicasso/hermes-jev-curator (jev-curator v0.1.0)**, is an upstream community semantic governance plugin (currently an experimental v0.1.0 release validated against a 21-case synthetic contract self-check) that imports stock Hermes Agent modules (tools.skill\_usage, agent.skill\_utils, agent.curator\_backup, tools.write\_approval) in a strictly read-only manner without patching core code11. It constructs star-shaped direct-edge skill merge plans after a 60-second quiet-minute debounce and blocks unauthorized background destructive skill\_manage mutations22.  
Third, the **upstream submodule (.hermes/hermes-agent)** reports clean via git status against official NousResearch/hermes-agent2. Furthermore, to replace any external benchmark routing glue when switching models on Port 8642, upstream NousResearch/hermes-agent natively provides gateway.platforms.api\_server.model\_routes in config.yaml, which deterministically maps incoming model aliases to specific (provider, model) pairs without custom Python interceptor code25.  
![][image13]

### **5.2 Forensic Scrutiny of private\_dot\_hermes/config.yaml and Upstream Flag Mechanics**

We now evaluate every section of the active private\_dot\_hermes/config.yaml (\_config\_version: 44\) against upstream NousResearch/hermes-agent source mechanics (agent/prompt\_builder.py, agent/system\_prompt.py, gateway/platforms/api\_server.py) and the four audit questions posed in Document 411.  
First, regarding **Model Selection (model.default)**, config.yaml currently specifies default: gemma-4-E4B-it-qat (Candidate 1\)1. Based on the empirical failure of Candidate 1 on Tau-Bench (0.0%), its 74.74% multi-token identifier mutation risk, and its 68°C operating temperature, model.default must be updated to **nemotron-3.5-bolt-e4b** (Tier 1B Primary Agent OS Champion), while retaining **gemma-4-E4B-it-qat-exact** (Tier 1A Specialist) as a named route under gateway.platforms.api\_server.model\_routes for Stage 03 (03-execute) AST and coding tasks3.  
Second, regarding the **Agent Guidance Flags (tool\_use\_enforcement: false, execution\_guidance: false, task\_completion\_guidance: false, parallel\_tool\_call\_guidance: false)**, upstream source forensics (Issues \#56360, \#28079, and \#96550) confirm why these flags must remain false for local quantized models on Port 864211. As documented in upstream **Issue \#56360**, when serving a local OpenAI-compatible model via api\_server (Port 8642), enabling tool\_use\_enforcement, task\_completion\_guidance, and parallel\_tool\_call\_guidance injects **7,237 characters of boilerplate prose** (8,866 chars total vs. 1,629 chars persona-only) into the stable system prompt layer64. Quantized local models interpret the prose instructions in \# Tool-use enforcement ("you MUST make the corresponding tool call...") literally and print tool calls as **raw text inside message.content** (such as \<tool\_call\>{"name": ...}) instead of emitting native structured OpenAI tool\_calls, or fabricate execution results64. Disabling those flags in Issue \#56360 restored **20/20 non-streaming and 10/10 streaming structured tool call reliability with zero text leaks**64. Similarly, in agent/prompt\_builder.py (Upstream **Issue \#96550**), OPENAI\_MODEL\_EXECUTION\_GUIDANCE (execution\_guidance) is a 12-line block that auto mode already excludes for gemini/gemma architectures65. In Hermes Agent OS, **Jake Van Clief's ICM Layer 1/2 markdown files (AGENTS.md, CONTEXT.md, invariants.md, rules.md) replace generic upstream boilerplate with explicit, stage-specific contracts**, saving \~1,800 tokens of prompt overhead on every turn11. However, we recommend raising agent.max\_turns from 25 to **40** so multi-order audits (like Tau-Bench Task 2\) have sufficient turn headroom without hitting iteration\_budget\_exhausted3.  
Third, regarding **Tiered Tool Search (tools.tool\_search.enabled: "off")**, upstream documentation (website/docs/user-guide/features/tool-search.md) specifies that built-in \_HERMES\_CORE\_TOOLS (terminal, read\_file, write\_file, patch, search\_files, todo, memory, web\_search, execute\_code, delegate\_task) **never defer** under any tool\_search setting63. Only MCP and non-core plugin tools (openviking's 6 viking\_\* tools and jev-curator's jev\_skill\_relations tool—7 small tools total) are eligible for deferral20. When tool\_search is set to "auto" or "on", the presence of any deferrable plugin tool activates **Tier 1**, replacing the plugin tool schemas with 3 bridge tools (tool\_search, tool\_describe, tool\_call)63. Invoking any deferred tool then requires **1 to 2 extra LLM round-trips** (tool\_describe → tool\_call), and deferred schemas loaded into conversation history **do not benefit from system-prompt KV prefix caching**63. Because Hermes attaches only 7 lightweight plugin tools (\~600 tokens total, which remain cached in the stable prefix at a **99.8% cache hit rate**), keeping tools.tool\_search.enabled: "off" is optimal for both production ICM stages and Layer B benchmarks3.  
Fourth, regarding **Context Length (context\_length: 131072\)**, all models under providers.local-llama.models specify 131072, matching \-c 131072 \-ctk q4\_0 \-ctv q4\_0 on Port 8138 and preventing the 32K context floor crash in agent\_init.py1.

### **5.3 Canonical Production private\_dot\_hermes/config.yaml Specification (v45 Upgrade)**

Below is the certified private\_dot\_hermes/config.yaml upgrade incorporating the Tier 1B Champion default, removal of decommissioned Candidate 1, declarative api\_server.model\_routes stage routing, and jev-curator semantic governance:

YAML  
\# \~/.hermes/config.yaml — Certified GDR30 Production Configuration  
\_config\_version: 45

model:  
  provider: local-llama  
  default: nemotron-3.5-bolt-e4b  
  base\_url: http\://127.0.0.1:8138/v1  
  context\_length: 131072

providers:  
  local-llama:  
    api: http\://127.0.0.1:8138/v1  
    api\_key\_env: LOCAL\_LLAMA\_API\_KEY  
    stale\_timeout\_seconds: 120  
    models:  
      nemotron-3.5-bolt-e4b:  
        context\_length: 131072  
        max\_output\_tokens: 4096  
      gemma-4-E4B-it-qat-exact:  
        context\_length: 131072  
        max\_output\_tokens: 4096  
  local-embedding-cpu:  
    api: http\://127.0.0.1:8139/v1  
    api\_key\_env: LOCAL\_EMBEDDING\_API\_KEY  
    models:  
      embeddinggemma-2-q8\_0:  
        context\_length: 8192  
        dimensions: 768

\# Declarative Fix for Upstream Issues \#56360 & \#81670:  
\# Eliminates 7.2 KB of boilerplate prompt bloat and prevents raw-text tool leaks on Port 8642\.  
\# Stage behavioral constraints are supplied by ICM Layer 1/2 markdown files (AGENTS.md / CONTEXT.md).  
agent:  
  tool\_use\_enforcement: false  
  execution\_guidance: false  
  task\_completion\_guidance: false  
  parallel\_tool\_call\_guidance: false  
  max\_turns: 40

\# Declarative Gateway & Zero-Code Stage Model Routing (Port 8642\)  
gateway:  
  host: 127.0.0.1  
  port: 8642  
  platforms:  
    api\_server:  
      enabled: true  
      extra:  
        direct\_model\_requests: true  
      model\_routes:  
        hermes-agent:  
          provider: local-llama  
          model: nemotron-3.5-bolt-e4b  
        icm-tier1b-policy:  
          provider: local-llama  
          model: nemotron-3.5-bolt-e4b  
        icm-tier1a-coding:  
          provider: local-llama  
          model: gemma-4-E4B-it-qat-exact

\# Core tools are always eager; keeping tool\_search "off" preserves 99.8% KV prefix cache hits  
\# across the 7 lightweight OpenViking/Jev plugin tools without extra tool\_describe round-trips.  
tools:  
  tool\_search:  
    enabled: "off"  
    threshold\_pct: 4  
    listing\_max\_tokens: 1200

lsp:  
  enabled: true  
  servers:  
    pyright:  
      disabled: false

\# Official OpenViking Hierarchical Memory Plugin (Port 1933, CPU Embeddings on Port 8139\)  
memory:  
  provider: openviking  
  openviking:  
    url: http\://127.0.0.1:1933  
    embedding\_provider: local-embedding-cpu  
    embedding\_model: embeddinggemma-2-q8\_0  
    matryoshka\_dim: 256

\# Upstream Semantic Skill Governance (anpicasso/hermes-jev-curator)  
plugins:  
  enabled:  
    \- openviking  
    \- jev-curator  
  entries:  
    jev-curator:  
      settings:  
        mode: guard  
        allow\_content\_egress: false

approvals:  
  mode: "off"

skills:  
  ledger: true  
  ledger\_max\_bytes: 5242880  
  write\_approval: false  
  external\_dirs:  
    \- \~/.agents/skills  
    \- \~/.hermes/skills
